title: Chapter 57: Ashes on Lantern Quay, Part 1 of 5: The Fourth Desk at Dawn
html:
The Auditor of the Fourth Desk had not slept.
She sat at her window on the third floor of the Oblivion Bank with her coat still on and her gloves still on and watched the smoke.
It was the hour before dawn. The hour when the night is at its coldest and its darkest, and the lamps on Lantern Quay below her window burn their steadiest, and the river goes by under them black and slow and silent, carrying the ice down to the sea. She had watched it at this hour many times. She did not sleep well. She had not slept well for six years. She had a chair by this window, a hard wooden chair with a cushion that Mister Gage had brought her once without a word, and on the nights when she did not sleep she sat in it and watched the river and the lamps and the dark shapes of the barges moored along the quay, and waited for the gray to come up over the roofs on the other side of the water.
Tonight there was no gray.
Tonight there was a glow.
It was over the roofs to the north and west. Over the Exchange. Low down, close to the rooftops, a dull dark red, like the inside of a stove when the fire has burned down. And above the red, the smoke. A great slow column of it, going up into the black sky. Not black smoke. Gray. Pale gray, almost white, lit from below by the red glow, so that it looked like a pillar of cloud standing on the city. It went up and up, and at the top, very high, the wind off the sea caught it and bent it over, and it spread out eastward across the sky in a long flat gray sheet, over the river, over Lantern Quay, over the Bank. And out of the sheet, very softly, something was falling.
Not snow. The snow had stopped an hour ago.
Ash.
It came down past her window in the lamplight. Fine and gray and light, turning over and over, the way snow turns. It settled on the stone sill outside the glass. It settled on the lamps of the quay, and on the decks of the barges, and on the black water of the river, where it lay for a moment, gray, on the surface, and then went dark and sank. It had been falling for two hours. The quay was gray with it. The roofs across the water were gray with it. When she had come up the steps of the Bank at the third bell, with Gage behind her, it had been on her shoulders and in her hair, and when she had brushed it off in the hall it had left her white gloves gray.
She had not washed them.
She did not know why. She looked down at them now, in her lap. Her white kid gloves, gray at the fingertips and on the backs of the hands, where she had brushed the ash away. She had a drawer full of clean ones. She had not changed them.
It was the ash of the Memory Bourse. She knew that. Everybody on the quay knew it. The night porter had told her, at the door, with his face white. The Lady's house, Miss. On the Exchange. All of it. They say the dome came down.
She had known before he told her. She had been there when it came down.
The Auditor took off her right glove.
She did it slowly, a finger at a time. And put the glove on the windowsill, on the inside of the glass, where the gray ash from the outside could not reach it. And looked at her bare hand.
It was a thin hand. Pale. Clean. The nails cut short and square. A clerk's hand. A hand that had held a pen for six years, every day, from the first bell to the eighth, and sometimes later. There was a small hard bump on the side of the second finger, where the pen rested, and a faint blue stain in the skin under it that never quite washed out. That was all. There was nothing else on it. No ring. No scar. Nothing to say whose hand it had been before.
She had looked at it many times. In this chair. At this hour. She did not know what she was looking for.
On the little table beside her chair there was a book.
It was small and black and very worn, the corners rubbed round, the spine cracked in a dozen places and mended with thread. It was not a Bank book. It had no number on it and no lock and no green ink. It was hers. She carried it everywhere. In the inside pocket of her dark green coat, against her ribs, the way some people carry a letter.
She opened it.
The first page said, in her own small neat hand, very faded now:
I do not remember anything from before the morning of the ninth of the Thaw month, six years ago. This book is for counting what I lose from now on. So that at least I will know how much.
And under it, the count.
Page after page of it. Small neat figures, in rows, like a ledger. A date. A number. A few words. Used the Sight on the Harlow account. One day. The day before yesterday is gone. And the next. Used the Sight on the Farrier's Row deed. One day. A Tuesday. And the next. Page after page. Six years. Every time she had laid her bare hand on a page of a ledger and looked into it with the thing that the Bank called Ledger-Sight, and seen what was written under the writing, the truth under the lie, the hand that had held the pen. Every time, one day of her own life had gone out of her. Burned. Like a page torn out of a book. Never to come back.
She turned to the last page with writing on it.
The last line said: Running total: 2,409 days.
Two thousand four hundred and nine days. More than six years. More days than she had lived since the morning of the ninth of the Thaw month. She had been burning them faster than she could make them. For a long time now she had not been able to remember last week. Last month was a gray blur. Last year, almost nothing. She lived in the present the way a woman lives on a raft at sea, with nothing behind her and nothing ahead, only the boards under her feet and the water all round.
And the book.
She took a pencil from the table, and wrote under the last line.
Midwinter. The Bourse. Did not use the Sight. Lost nothing.
She looked at it.
Then she wrote another line under it.
Found something.
She looked at that for a long time.
She had not meant to write it. Her hand had written it. The way her hand sometimes did things before she had decided to do them. Kept a pair of gray-dirty gloves on when she had clean ones. Took two folded barley-sugar wrappers off a windowsill in a stranger's empty room on Tallow Street, in the autumn, and put them in her coat, and never threw them away.
She did not know what she had found. She did not have a word for it. It was not a thing. It was not a fact. It was not anything she could write in a ledger or weigh on a scale or file in a drawer under a number. It was a—
She did not know what it was.
It had come to her in the light. The great white light, coming up out of the hole in the floor of the dome, after the dome came down. She had been standing in the kitchen passage with Gage's arm round her, and the light had come up, and for a hundred breaths she had—
She shut the book.
Not yet. She would think about it later. When she had slept. When it was light. When she could look at it in the day and see what it was, and not in the dark, at this hour, with the ash coming down past the window and her bare hand in her lap and the river going by.
Behind her, in the dark of the Fourth Desk, something creaked.
She did not turn round. She knew what it was.
The Fourth Desk was a long room. Long and narrow and low, with a row of tall windows on the river side, and a row of tall cupboards on the other, all the way down, black wood, locked, with brass numbers on the doors. Between them, three desks. Her own, at the far end, by her window. A clerk's desk in the middle, where Mister Harrow sat from the first bell to the eighth with his green ledger and his ink. And by the door, a bench. A long bench of bare oak, with nothing on it.
That was Gage's.
He was sitting on it now. In the dark. She had not lit a lamp. He had not asked her to. He had come up the stairs behind her at the third bell, and when she sat down in her chair by the window, he had sat down on his bench by the door, and he had not moved since. She had heard him breathing. Slow and deep and even, like the sea. He did not sleep either. She did not think he ever slept. She had never once in six years come into the Fourth Desk, at any hour of the day or night, and found Mister Gage not sitting on his bench by the door.
He was a very big man. Bigger than anybody she knew. So big that he had to duck his head to come through the door, and turn his shoulders to come up the stairs. He had a broad, flat, plain face, like a face cut out of wood with a few strokes of a knife, and small gray eyes, and no hair at all. He wore a gray coat that the Bank tailor had had to make for him specially, with twice the cloth. And round his neck, on a cord, he wore a slate. A small square school slate, in a wooden frame, with a stub of chalk tied to it on a string.
He did not speak. He had never spoken, not once, in six years. He wrote on the slate. Not often. Only when it mattered. And then he wiped it clean with the side of his great hand, and let it hang on its cord against his chest again, blank.
She did not know where he had come from. She did not know his first name. She did not know who had sent him, or why, or how long he had been with her before the morning of the ninth of the Thaw month, when she woke up in the narrow bed in the room at the top of the Bank with no memory of anything, and he had been sitting on a stool by the door. Waiting. With his slate.
The first thing he had ever written on it, that morning, was: Your name is Elara. You are the Auditor. I am Gage.
And she had believed him.
She had never been sure why.
The bench creaked again.
And then there was the small dry scratch of chalk on slate. In the dark. Slow. A few letters. And then a pause. And then the scratch again.
She waited.
She heard him get up. Slowly, the way a big man gets up, in stages. And come down the long dark room toward her, between the desks, his great soft boots silent on the boards. He stopped beside her chair. She could feel the size of him there in the dark, like a wall.
He held the slate down beside her, low, by the window, so that the lamplight from the quay below fell on it.
She looked at it.
You should sleep.
"I know," she said.
He did not take the slate away. He wiped it with the side of his hand, and wrote again, slowly, while she watched. The chalk squeaked a little on the slate.
He was there. Last night.
The Auditor sat very still.
She did not ask who. She did not have to.
She had seen him. She had not known, until this moment, that she had seen him. But she had. At the eleventh bell, in the dome, from her little table by the brass box, with her lamp and her inkstand and her ledger. A lame old cellarman in Bourse livery, with a heavy face and a mole under his left eye, pouring wine for the Duke of Marrow. She had looked at him across the floor, once, because his hands were wrong. A cellarman's hands should be red and rough and cracked from the cold of the cellar. His were in white gloves. Clean white cotton gloves, too clean, with something gray showing at the wrists when he reached for the decanter.
She had looked at the gray at his wrists. And something in her had gone still, the way it went still when she laid her bare hand on a page and felt the lie under it.
And then the Weigher had called the next lot, and she had looked down at her ledger, and when she looked up again, the cellarman was gone.
He was there, said the slate.
"I know," said the Auditor.
She looked at the slate for a long time. Then she looked up at Gage. At the plain wooden face, very high above her in the dark, with the lamplight from the quay on its underside.
"Did he get out?" she said.
Gage looked down at her.
Then he wiped the slate, and wrote one word, and held it down for her to see.
Yes.
She let out a breath.
She had not known she was holding it. She let it out, and it went out of her in a long white cloud against the cold glass of the window, and fogged it, and through the fog the red glow over the Exchange and the gray column of smoke went soft and blurred, like a picture seen through tears.
She did not know why it mattered.
She did not know who he was. Not really. A name on a list. A name scratched into the wall by a bed in that same empty room on Tallow Street. CORIN VANE. OAKHAVEN. ELARA. Three words. She had written them in her black book, in the autumn, and looked at them every day since. And in the autumn, in that room, with her bare hand on the wall, she had heard a man's voice and a little girl laughing.
That was all.
It was not nothing.
"Thank you," she said to Gage.
He wiped the slate. And let it hang. And did not go back to his bench. He stood beside her chair in the dark, very big and very still, and looked out of the window with her at the smoke going up over the city. And the ash came down past the glass, gray, turning over and over, and settled on the sill.
After a while, over the roofs on the other side of the river, the gray came up at last.
It was dawn.
Clause Eleven
She had been at the box at midnight. That was her work. That was clause eleven.
Clause eleven of the Charter of the Memory Bourse, which the Lady's mother had signed with the Bank forty years ago, in green ink, on a sheet of vellum that was kept in a cupboard in the Fourth Desk with a brass 11 on its door. It was a short clause. Six lines. The Auditor had read it so many times she could say it with her eyes shut.
Any lot of the Fourth Tier, being a thing of more than common weight, shall be weighed by the Bank before sale and held by the Bank's officer during sale, and the box of sealed bids for such lots shall not be opened save in the presence of the Auditor of the Fourth Desk, who shall record the bids and the winner, and whose record shall stand.
Whose record shall stand.
That was why she had been there. In the dome. At a small table by the brass box on its iron pillar, from the ninth bell to midnight, with a lamp and an inkstand and a ledger bound in green leather. Not as a guest. Not in a mask. In her dark green coat and her white gloves, with her hair pinned flat, the way she wore it every day at the Fourth Desk. A clerk at a party. The lords had looked at her the way you look at a clock on a wall. And then not looked at her again.
She had liked that. She had always liked being looked at like a clock.
She had sat at her small table and watched the floor of the dome all evening. The lords and ladies in their masks. The glass tables with the glowing lots on plum velvet. The Weigher, tall and thin and very old, in his near-black coat with his silver scale on its chain, calling the lots. The cards, white with a plum border, going into the slot of the brass box one by one, like leaves falling into a well. She had marked every card in her ledger as it went in. Not the bid. She could not see the bid. Only the card. Lot 9. One card. Sponsor, the Langley house. Eleventh bell and a quarter. That was the rule.
She had seen the Treasurer drop a card. Dorian Sterling, in gray silk with silver thread, with his silver hair and his black eyes and his gold watch chain. A card he had written before he came. He had dropped it into the slot without looking at it, and then turned and spoken to her. Pleasantly. A long night for you, Miss Elara. And then looked across the floor at the Archon, and bowed, and touched his watch chain. She had written it down. Lot 41. One card. Sponsor, the Treasurer's office.
She had seen the Archon's secretary drop a card. Lucian. Five steps from the Archon's chair to the box. Five steps back. She had written that down too. Lot 41. One card. Sponsor, the Council. By the hand of the Archon's secretary.
She had seen the Inquisitor take no card at all.
She had written that down.
And at a quarter to midnight the Lady had come down the great stair, with a servant carrying her train, and had not bowed to the Archon. The Auditor had seen that. Everybody had seen it. The whole dome had drawn its breath at once, like a single great animal, when the Lady came down the last step and walked past the Archon's chair without bending her head, and went to the brass box, and struck it once with her black lace fan.
The Fourth Tier.
And the floor had sunk.
The ring of black squares round the box's iron pillar, going down like a lid into a well, with a groan of chain on a drum, somewhere far below. And the cold coming up. The cold of the ice cellar, and the smell of sealed jars. The Auditor had felt it on her face. She had not moved. She had held her pen over her ledger, and written: Quarter to midnight. The floor opened.
And then the Fourth Tier lots had come up on the lift, one by one. Lot 39, A War, in a great dark jar that seemed to drink the light round it. Lot 40, A Marriage, two small jars bound together with a gold wire. And Lot 41.
Last.
A black wooden case with silver corners and a silver clasp shaped like a closed hand, sitting alone in the middle of a velvet tray.
She had looked at it, on its tray, across the black ring of the open floor. And she had known it.
She had weighed it. On the Thursday before last, in the cold room under the floor, with the Lady's man Gant holding the lantern and Gage standing behind her. That was the first part of clause eleven. Shall be weighed by the Bank before sale. She had put on her white gloves and lifted it off its shelf and set it on the Bank's own brass scale, the one that went with her everywhere in a leather case, and watched the needle swing and settle. And she had written the weight in her green ledger, in a figure so small and so exact that nobody but the Fourth Desk would ever be able to read it.
And she had done something else, that Thursday. Something that was not in clause eleven.
She had taken off her right glove, and laid her bare hand on the black wood of the lid.
Only for a moment. Only for a breath. She had not meant to. Her hand had done it. And she had not used the Sight. She was sure of that. She had not looked into it. She had only touched it. And through the cold black wood, under her bare palm, she had felt—
She did not know what she had felt.
Something folded. Something folded very small, and very tight, and held. Like a hand that has been closed round a thing for so long it has forgotten how to open.
She had taken her hand away. And put her glove back on. And written the weight in her ledger. And Gant had held the lantern and noticed nothing, and Gage had stood behind her, and when she turned round he had been looking at her with his small gray eyes, and he had not written anything on his slate. Not then. Not afterward.
That was the case on the velvet tray.
And the Weigher had called it.
Lot forty-one. A Lord's Last Evening. Taken whole. Before the fire.
And the whole dome had leaned forward.
And at the twelfth bell, the Lady had opened the box.
She had done it with a small brass key on a ribbon round her wrist. The Auditor had stood beside her. That was the rule. Close beside her, at her left hand, with her green ledger open on her arm and her pen ready. The Lady had unlocked the brass box, and lifted its heavy lid, and the cards had been there inside it, all of them, white with plum borders, lying in a heap at the bottom like fallen leaves. And the Lady had put her long pale hand in, and stirred them, and taken them out one by one, and read them aloud in her high cracked painted voice. And the Auditor had written each one down.
The lots of the first three tiers went quickly. A name. A sum. Sold. The Weigher's small hammer on the wood. The Auditor's pen.
Then the Fourth Tier.
Lot thirty-nine. A War. The Duke of Ashcombe's house, four thousand crowns.
Lot forty. A Marriage. The Pellow house, two thousand.
And then the Lady's hand had gone into the box again, and come out with two cards. Only two. And she had looked at them. For a long moment. The Auditor, standing at her left hand, had seen her look. Had seen the long pale painted face go quite still, the way the Auditor's own face went still when she touched a lie.
Lot forty-one, the Lady had said. A Lord's Last Evening.
She had read the first card.
The Treasurer's office. Ten thousand crowns.
A sound had gone round the dome. Not a gasp. Lower than that. The sound of a great many people who had never in their lives heard of ten thousand crowns being paid for anything at all.
The Auditor had written it down. Her hand had not shaken. Lot 41. Treasurer's office. 10,000.
And the Lady had read the second card.
She had not read it aloud at once. She had held it in her long pale fingers and looked at it, and the Auditor, at her left hand, had seen what was written on it. There was no sum. There was no name. There was only a mark. Drawn in black ink, very neatly, in the middle of the white card with the plum border.
A circle.
A small, plain, perfect circle.
The Council, the Lady had said, at last. And her painted voice had been quite steady. By the hand of the Archon. No sum is named.
And she had looked up from the card, across the hole in the floor, at the plain high-backed chair beside the box, where the man in the black half-mask sat with his black-gloved hands resting on the flat dark case on his knees. The case with four round hollows in its lid.
Clause eleven, the Lady had said, does not say that a sum must be named.
Nobody had said anything.
The Auditor had looked at the circle on the card. And then she had looked at her ledger, open on her arm. At the line she had to write. The line whose record would stand.
She had written it.
Lot 41. The Council, by the hand of the Archon. No sum named. Winner.
And the Lady had said, Sold, and the Weigher had struck his hammer on the wood, once, and the sound of it had gone up into the great glass dome over their heads and come back down, very small.
And at that moment, at the bronze doors, the ram.
She remembered it the way you remember a door slamming in a dream. Boom. And the whole dome going still. Boom. And the bronze doors bending in at the middle, very slightly, the way a sheet of paper bends when you push it with a finger. Boom. And then the doors flying open. And the men in gray.
She had not moved. That was the strange thing. She remembered that very clearly. The Lady had turned, and the Weigher had turned, and every lord and lady in the dome had turned toward the doors and begun to scream. And the Auditor had stood at the Lady's left hand by the open brass box with her green ledger on her arm and her pen in her fingers and had not moved at all. Because she had been looking at the Archon.
And the Archon had not moved either.
He had sat in his plain high-backed chair by the box with his hands on the case on his knees, and his black half-mask turned toward the bronze doors. Watching the men in gray come in. Not surprised. Not afraid. The way a man watches a clock strike an hour he has been waiting for.
And then he had stood up.
He had handed the flat dark case with the four hollows to Lucian, without looking at him. And said something to him. Very low. The Auditor had not heard what. And Lucian had bowed, and gone, not toward the bronze doors, but toward the edge of the hole. Toward the velvet tray on top of the iron pillar beside the box. Toward the black case with the silver clasp.
And the Archon had turned and walked away. Not hurrying. Across the black and white floor, through the screaming lords, who fell back from him on both sides the way water falls back from the bow of a ship. To the small plain door in the curve of the wall to the right of the bronze doors. The garden door. Where he had come in at the ninth bell.
And gone out through it.
The Auditor had watched him go.
And then she had looked down at her ledger, at the line she had just written. Winner. And then she had looked across the hole at the velvet tray, and at Lucian lifting the black case off it in both arms, carefully, against his chest.
And she had known.
Not with the Sight. With her eyes. Across twelve paces of black nothing, in the lamplight, with the screaming all round her. She had looked at the black case in Lucian's arms and known, the way you know your own handwriting, that it was not the case she had weighed on the Thursday before last.
It was too light. Not by much. A breath. A hair. She could see it in the way Lucian held it. In the way his arms did not bend quite as far as they should. In the way the silver corners caught the lamplight a fraction higher than they ought to have.
She had weighed four thousand things in six years. She knew what things weighed.
And then the first lamp had burst.
